source: The same cohort also underwent a 2-bottle choice test in which mice similarly discriminated 4% from 20% sucrose (2-way-ANOVA: no interaction; main effect of Sucrose concentration: F (1, 36)=11.11, p=0.002); main effect of Treatment: F (1, 36)=8.421, p=0.006) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of two-bottle choice test with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Altered sucrose perception does not contribute to the pattern of findings following OFC inhibition.
source: Overall, these data suggest that altered sucrose perception does not contribute to the pattern of current findings following OFC inhibition.
evidence: Interpretation of the two-bottle choice test results.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PV interneurons inhibited OFC projection neuron spiking for 5 s, with no evidence of an increase in rebound firing post light activation.
source: We verified our ability to induce an inhibitory clamp on OFC projections ex vivo, where in whole-cell recordings we saw optogenetic activation of PV interneurons inhibited projection neuron spiking for 5 s, with no evidence of an increase in rebound firing post light activation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Electrophysiological recording data with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Light delivery and the subsequent inhibition of OFC projection neurons had little effect on anticipatory and consummatory licking behaviors exhibited across the re-exposure session.
source: Light delivery and the subsequent inhibition of OFC projection neurons had little effect on anticipatory and consummatory licking behaviors exhibited across the re-exposure session.
evidence: Summary statement about licking behavior with optogenetic manipulation.

claim: There was an interaction of Treatment x Time in licking rate across the session (2-way repeated measures ANOVA (Treatment x Time): F(5, 80)=2.54, p=0.035) and a main effect of Time (F(5, 80)=3.52, p=0.006) but not of Treatment (p=0.14).
source: When we looked at the licking rate across the session, we did see an interaction (2-way repeated measures ANOVA (Treatment x Time): F(5, 80)=2.54, p=0.035) and a main effect of Time (F(5, 80)=3.52, p=0.006) but not of Treatment (p=0.14) (Figure 5F)
evidence: Statistical analysis of licking rate with optogenetic manipulation and reference to Figure 5F.

claim: Light delivery during sucrose consumption produced an effect on the duration of the licking burst (unpaired t-test: t16 = 2.211, p=0.041).
source: When we evaluated consumption licking behavior (i.e. after an outcome delivery), we did see an effect of light delivery on the duration of the licking burst (unpaired t-test: t16 = 2.211, p=0.041) (Figure 5L).
evidence: Statistical analysis of burst duration with optogenetic manipulation and reference to Figure 5L.

claim: Light delivery during sucrose consumption did not grossly alter licking behavior in comparison to yoked controls.
source: Our data suggests that light delivery during sucrose consumption did not grossly alter licking behavior in comparison to our yoked controls.
evidence: Summary interpretation of licking behavior data with optogenetic manipulation.

claim: OFC inhibition during consumption leaves sucrose palatability largely intact.
source: It appears OFC inhibition during consumption leaves sucrose palatability largely intact.
evidence: Interpretation of licking behavior data with optogenetic manipulation.

claim: Yoked mice significantly reduced test response rates from acquisition baseline (one-sample t-test against 100% baseline: t7 = 3.07, p=0.018).
source: Yoked mice significantly reduced test response rates from acquisition baseline (one-sample t-test against 100% baseline: t7 = 3.07, p=0.018)
evidence: Statistical test comparing response rate to baseline in yoked control group.

claim: ChR2 mice showed a trend toward reduced test response rates from acquisition baseline (t7 = 2.20, p=0.06).
source: while ChR2 mice did less so (t7 = 2.20, p=0.06).
evidence: Statistical test comparing response rate to baseline in ChR2 group.

claim: Six out of eight pairs of ChR2 mice and their yoked control showed a decreased response rate in yoked versus ChR2 mice, although the group difference was not significant (paired t-test: t5 = 1.67, p=0.14).
source: Six out of eight pairs of ChR2 mice and their yoked control showed a decreased response rate in yoked versus ChR2 mice, although the group difference was not significant (paired t-test: t5 = 1.67, p=0.14).
evidence: Statistical comparison between ChR2 and yoked groups.

claim: OFC inhibition during sucrose experience decreases value updating.
source: Our data suggest that OFC inhibition during sucrose experience decreases value updating.
evidence: Interpretation of the optogenetic manipulation results.

claim: Yoked mice showed evidence that they had updated a decrease in outcome value corresponding to experiencing sucrose in a decreased motivational state, and ChR2 mice did not.
source: Importantly, Yoked mice showed evidence that they had updated a decrease in outcome value corresponding to experiencing sucrose in a decreased motivational state, and ChR2 mice did not.
evidence: Interpretation comparing the two groups in the optogenetic experiment.

claim: OFC inhibition overlapping with sucrose experience interferes with the ability to update value, while OFC inhibition not explicitly paired with sucrose consumption does not.
source: While our data does not speak to how much sucrose experience is necessary to be able to update value changes, our data does suggest that OFC inhibition overlapping with sucrose experience interferes with the ability to update, while OFC inhibition not explicitly paired with sucrose consumption does not.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the optogenetic manipulation experiment.

claim: The OFC is involved in updating value changes subsequently used to control decision-making, highlighting the contribution of OFC to model-based action control.
source: Here we find that the OFC is involved in updating value changes subsequently used to control decision-making, highlighting the contribution of OFC to model-based action control.
evidence: Summary conclusion of the study's main finding.

claim: OFC projection neurons are necessary to learn relative value changes that are subsequently used to inform goal-directed behavior.
source: We found OFC projection neurons are necessary to learn relative value changes that are subsequently used to inform goal-directed behavior.
evidence: Summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: OFC activity was necessary to encode both decreases and increases in relative value, independent of the valence of the motivational state change.
source: Importantly, this is independent of the valence of the motivational state change, as OFC activity was necessary to encode both decreases and increases in relative value.
evidence: Summary of findings from both positive and negative incentive learning experiments.

claim: The finding that OFC activity is necessary for both increases and decreases in value contradicts previous hypotheses suggesting a role for OFC in behavioral disinhibition.
source: The latter finding contradicts previous hypotheses suggesting a role for OFC in behavioral disinhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation that contrasts the current findings with prior hypotheses.

claim: OFC performs computations based on sensory information directly gained from the consumption experience.
source: Further, our finding for the necessity of OFC activity when directly experiencing value changes suggests that OFC performs computations based on sensory information directly gained from the consumption experience.
evidence: Interpretation of the optogenetic manipulation findings.

claim: OFC has been implicated in direct sensory and gustatory processing.
source: In light of OFC's prior implications in direct sensory and gustatory processing (Grabenhorst et al., 2008; Lara et al., 2009; Ohla et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: OFC updates value changes from an experienced aspect derived from sensory information.
source: we hypothesize OFC updates value changes from an experienced aspect derived from sensory information.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and prior literature.

claim: Model-based learning requires the ability to readily update associative information then used to infer the most appropriate action.
source: Model-based learning requires the ability to readily update associative information then used to infer the most appropriate action.
evidence: This is a statement about established concepts in the field.

claim: Optogenetic activation of lOFC only during testing selectively increases goal-directed actions.
source: Previous work has shown that optogenetic activation of lOFC only during testing selectively increases goal-directed actions (Gremel and Costa, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Precise optogenetic OFC inhibition prevented value updating in a Pavlovian task.
source: while precise optogenetic OFC inhibition prevented value updating in a Pavlovian task (Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: lOFC activity is necessary for value updating in a decision-making task characterized as model-based control.
source: Our present data adds to this literature by showing the lOFC activity is necessary for value updating in a decision-making task characterized as model-based control.
evidence: Summary of how the current findings contribute to existing literature.

claim: Mechanisms within lOFC support both model-based learning as well as the ability to infer such changes to support decision-making.
source: These data suggest that mechanisms within lOFC support both model-based learning as well as the ability to infer such changes to support decision-making.
evidence: Interpretation of the current findings in the context of OFC function.

claim: OFC is not necessary for perceiving changes in palatability.
source: While our data supports a crucial role for OFC in updating value representations supporting model-based behavior, our data also adds to recent findings that show OFC is not necessary for perceiving changes in palatability (Gardner et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of findings with reference to recent literature.

claim: Broadly attenuating OFC projection neuron activity or temporally inhibiting OFC projection neuron activity did little to change appetitive and consummatory licking behaviors.
source: Broadly attenuating OFC projection neuron activity or temporally inhibiting OFC projection neuron activity did little to change appetitive and consummatory licking behaviors (Figures 3–5).
evidence: Summary of licking behavior results with references to multiple figures.

claim: Mice with OFC attenuated were still able to retrieve the sucrose representation.
source: This suggests that mice with OFC attenuated were still able to retrieve the sucrose representation.
evidence: Interpretation of the licking behavior data.

claim: OFC attenuation did not affect retrieval of the sucrose representation used to initiate the first appetitive lick.
source: The lack of a difference suggests that OFC attenuation did not affect retrieval of the sucrose representation used to initiate the first appetitive lick (Figures 3G and 4D).
evidence: Interpretation of latency to lick data with references to figures.

claim: Updating value representations under novel circumstances can be used to infer consequences for appropriate decision-making, as re-exposure happening outside of the training context was sufficient to update the representation.
source: The present incentive learning data suggests that updating value representations under novel circumstances can be used to infer consequences for appropriate decision-making, as re-exposure happening outside of the training context was sufficient to update the representation (Figure 1M).
evidence: Interpretation of the context experiment with reference to Figure 1M.

claim: OFC activity was intact the majority of the session during optogenetic inhibition experiments.
source: We do know that given the precise timing of the inhibition manipulation, OFC activity was intact the majority of the session.
evidence: Statement about the experimental design of the optogenetic manipulation.

claim: OFC inhibition did not prevent any additional motivational processes that might occur after the direct consummatory experience from contributing to the sucrose value representation.
source: OFC inhibition did not prevent any additional motivational processes that might occur after the direct consummatory experience (e.g., lasting pleasantness) from contributing to the sucrose value representation.
evidence: Interpretation of what the optogenetic manipulation did not affect.

claim: Accrued aspects of the sucrose consumption experience may be used to guide value updating processes.
source: Our data does suggest that accrued aspects of the sucrose consumption experience may be used to guide value updating processes.
evidence: Interpretation of the optogenetic manipulation findings.

claim: OFC is necessary for the updating of value under both positive and negative motivational states.
source: Here we have shown that OFC is necessary for the updating of value under both positive and negative motivational states.
evidence: Summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: This is the first experiment demonstrating OFC's role in retrieving and updating the value of an outcome and storing it for retrieval under a previously learned action contingency.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first experiment demonstrating OFC's role in retrieving and updating the value of an outcome and storing it for retrieval under a previously learned action contingency.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current findings.

claim: OFC has been hypothesized to function as an unobservable task state space.
source: OFC has been hypothesized to function as an unobservable task state space (Wilson et al., 2014; Schuck et al., 2016; Bradfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The current data offer support for the hypothesis that OFC functions as an unobservable task state space in model-based behavior.
source: Our data offer support for this hypothesis in model-based behavior.
evidence: Interpretation of how the current findings relate to prior hypotheses.

claim: In addition to the well-documented role OFC has in inferring value to control decision-making, mice also need OFC to update outcome representations.
source: We show that in addition to the well-documented role OFC has in inferring value to control decision-making, mice also need OFC to update outcome representations.
evidence: Summary of the dual role of OFC found in this study.

claim: During the re-exposure session, the unobservable component is the action portion of the action-outcome association.
source: During the re-exposure session, the unobservable component is the action portion of the action-outcome association.
evidence: Interpretation of the task design in the context of OFC function.

claim: OFC activity is necessary to update the outcome value used for inferring the value of the action.
source: Our data show that OFC activity is necessary to update the outcome value used for inferring the value of the action.
evidence: Summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: These studies provide insight into the role of orbitofrontal cortex in decision-making by showing a role for OFC in updating experienced-based changes in value.
source: In conclusion, these studies provide insight into the role of orbitofrontal cortex in decision-making by showing a role for OFC in updating experienced-based changes in value.
evidence: Concluding statement summarizing the contribution of the study.
